---
title: "Course 3 - Regression Models for Binary and Categorical Outcomes"
date: last-modified
---

Welcome to Biostatistics III. This week extends the regression workflow from Course 2 to **binary and categorical outcomes**. We will use logistic-regression models to answer clinical questions with estimated probabilities, probability differences, confidence intervals, and effect plots.

Odds ratios and log-odds appear often in psychiatric research papers, so we will learn what they mean. However, our primary interpretation will be on the **probability scale**: how much does the estimated probability of an outcome change, for whom, and with what uncertainty?

We will continue to work with the STePS randomised trial of internet-delivered psychodynamic therapy for social anxiety disorder. The course uses a post-treatment LSAS outcome grouped into low/no-to-mild, moderate/marked, and severe/very severe symptom categories. These are useful teaching categories; they are not presented as validated diagnostic or remission thresholds.

# Group work during lab sessions

Each afternoon, you will work in small groups in a Quarto notebook. The scenarios are intentionally a little under-specified—much like the analysis requests that arrive in a PhD—but every lab submission must include:

1. a clearly stated estimand or research question;
2. the model and important data decisions;
3. an uncertainty-aware probability-scale figure; and
4. a short clinical interpretation of the numerical result.

There is usually more than one defensible route through a lab. Discuss your choices, state what you conditioned on, and avoid treating a coefficient table as the analysis itself.

# Intended learning outcomes

After completing this course, you should be able to:

- define and fit binary logistic-regression models in R;
- distinguish probabilities, odds, log-odds, and odds ratios;
- communicate binary-model results as estimated probabilities and probability differences with 95% confidence intervals;
- use `marginaleffects` to estimate and visualise model-based predictions and contrasts;
- fit and interpret models with binary, categorical, and numeric predictors;
- interpret interaction models using conditional treatment effects on the probability scale; and
- reshape data to a long format and interpret multinomial-logit probabilities.

# Using AI tools

You may use generative AI tools in lab sessions. They can generate code that runs, but they can also generate confident statistical mistakes. You remain responsible for understanding the model, checking whether the code answers the stated question, and verifying every numerical claim before presenting it.
